Accepted29JAN2020
Acceptedarticleonline3FEB2020 1. Introduction
ThePaleo‐TethysOceanistypicallyreconstructedasatriangle‐shapedoceanbetweentheLaurasianand
GondwananplatesduringthePaleozoicandMesozoic(Sengör,1979).SinceLatePaleozoictime,aseries
of continental fragments(the Cimmerianterrane) began torift fromGondwana, and the convergence of
theseterranestowardLaurasialedtotheclosureofthePaleo‐TethysOcean(Metcalfe,2011;Sengör,1979;
Yin&Harrison,2000).Constrainingtheage,rate,andtectonicprocessesresponsibleforthedemiseofthe
eastern Paleo‐Tethys Ocean can improve our understanding of some major tectonics problems, such as
thecrustalassemblyandstructureoftheregionthatwouldmuchlaterbecometheTibetanPlateau.The
paleogeographyofthePaleo‐TethysOceanisalsorelevantforunderstandingthedistributionofcontinent
andmarineenvironmentsandbiogeography(Dewey&Burke,1973;Metcalfe,2011).
LargeuncertaintiesremaininthetimingoftheclosureofthePaleo‐TethysOcean.Estimatesfortheageof
oceanclosurerangewidely,fromtheMiddleJurassictoMiddleCretaceous(Yin&Harrison,2000),theLate
TriassictoEarlyJurassic(Dingetal.,2013;Rogeretal.,2010;Songetal.,2015),totheLatePermiantoEarly‐
MiddleTriassic(Jiangetal.,2013;Sha&Fursich,1999).Thekinematicsoftheoceanclosurearealsodis-
puted.AMediterranean‐styleclosuremodelofthePaleo‐TethysOceanwasfirstproposedbyPullenetal.
(2008)andthentestedandrefinedbydetritalzircondata(Dingetal.,2013)andgeochemicaldataofgran-
itoidsfromHoh‐Xil‐Songpan‐Ganzi(HXSG)basin(Zhangetal.,2014).InthisMediterranean‐stylemodel,a
Middle‐TriassiccollisionbetweenaPaleo‐TethysarcandthenorthernQiangtangblockoccurredpriortothe
LateTriassic‐EarlyJurassicfinalsuturingofthePaleo‐TethysOcean(Pullenetal.,2008).Anarc‐collision
mayhavereducedtheplateconvergenceratebetweenGondwana‐derivedblocksandLaurasia.However,
©2020.AmericanGeophysicalUnion.

thePaleo‐Tethysarcisinferredfromafewindirectgeologicalobservations,suchasuniquedetritalzircon

### page_2
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2019JB017804
agespectrafromthecentralQiangtangMetamorphicbelt(Pullenetal.,2008)andthedistributionofMiddle
TriassicmarinesedimentsinnorthernTibet(e.g.,Panetal.,2004).
Moregenerally,theclosureofthePaleo‐TethysOceanistheresultoftheaccretionoftheCimmerianter-
ranestowardtheEurasiaplate.ThenorthernQiangtangblockinCentralTibetisoneoftheseCimmerian
terranes and therefore is an important area to study the demise of the Paleo‐Tethys Ocean.
Paleomagnetism can provide quantitative estimates of latitude with time, from which minimum conver-
genceratescanbecalculatedandwhichcanprovideuniquekinematicinformationforreconstructingthe
tectonic evolution of the Tibetan Plateau (e.g., Bian et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2015;
Huang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016; Lippert et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2019; Tong et al., 2017;
Yan et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2016). Paleomagnetic data from
Paleozoic and Mesozoic rocks from the northern Qiangtang block are rare, but a recent paleomagnetic
study of the Late Triassic basaltic lavas of the northern Qiangtang block suggests that the final suturing
of the Paleo‐Tethys Ocean was complete prior to Late Triassic time (204–213 Ma) (Song et al., 2015). In
this paper, we describe new paleomagnetic data from Middle Triassic lavas and summarize published
paleomagnetic data from the northern Qiangtang block. These new and compiled observations help us
test the timing and kinematics of the closure of the Paleo‐Tethys Ocean. Given the age of our studied
rocks, we can also use these paleomagnetic data to test the arc‐continent collision model proposed by
Pullen et al. (2008).
2. Geological Setting andPaleomagnetic Sampling
TheTibetanPlateau,fromsouthtonorth,includestheTibetanHimalaya,Lhasa,Qiangtang,andKunlun‐
Qaidam blocks, separated by the Yarlung‐Zangpo, Bangong‐Nujiang, and Jinsha sutures, respectively
(Dingetal.,2013;Stampfli&Borel,2002).TheQiangtangblockisapproximately500to150kmwidefrom
itsmiddleparttoitseasternandwesternends(Figure1a).Alargeeast‐westtrendingbeltofMesozoictec-
tonic mélange containing high‐pressure and low‐temperature rocks is exposed in the central part of
Qiangtang. Some authors refer to this mélange belt as the Longmu Co‐Shuanghu suture, thereby distin-
guishing a southern and northern Qiangtang subblocks (Figure 1a) (Li, 1987; Zhang et al., 2006). Other
authors, however, argue that this mélange was subhorizontally underthrust southward from the Jinsha
suture and exhumed along low‐angle normal faults within the central Qiangtang terrane (Kapp et al.,
2000;Pullen&Kapp,2014);inthisinterpretation,itisimportanttonotethatthemélangedoesnotmake
aseparatesuturezonewithintheQiangtangterrane.
The Yidun arc is a microblock in eastern Tibet located between the Hoh‐Xil‐Songpan‐Ganzi (HXSG)
basin to the north and the northern Qiangtang block to the south. The Yidun arc complex consists of
Paleozoic limestones and mafic lavas and Triassic sediments, granitoids, and volcanic rocks (Wang
et al., 2011). The HXSG basin is composed mostlyof greenschist‐facies turbidites and other deep‐marine
facies of Triassic age (Ding et al., 2013; Yin & Nie, 1993). Lower Triassic shallow marine limestone and
interbedded conglomerates unconformably overlie Carboniferous‐Permian strata along the northern and
southern margins of the HXSG basin. The HXSG basin received ~2 × 106 km3 deep‐marine strata
during the Middle to Late Triassic (Ding et al., 2013; Yin & Nie, 1993). Three end‐member models have
beenproposedfortheformationoftheHXSGbasin:(1)aremanentoceanbasin(Zhou&Graham,1996);
(2) a rift basin (Chang, 2000); or (3) a Mediterranean‐style back‐arc basin (Ding et al., 2013; Klimetz,
1983; Pullen et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014). Each model reconstructs the Yidun arc south of the
HXSG during Triassic time, despite differences in the proposed origin of the Yidun arc: from the
Kunlun‐Qaidam block (Ding et al., 2013; Pullen et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014) or from the South
China block (Roger et al., 2010).
OurstudyarealiessouthofYanshipingtownonthenorthernQiangtangblock.Thislocationisbetween
the Jinsha suture and Longmucuo‐Shuanghu suture (Figure 1a). Mesozoic strata are abundant and out-
crop well at our study area and are mainly composed of the Jurassic Yanshiping Group and Triassic
BagongandBolilaFormations.TheTriassicBolilaFormationconsistsoflimestonesinterbeddedwithsilt-
stones and shales. The conformably overlying Triassic Bagong Formation is predominantly composed of
sandstones and siltstones. The Jurassic Yanshiping Group (comprising Quemoco, Buqu, Xiali, Suowa,
and Xueshan Formations), overlies the Bagong Formation in angular unconformity. Structurally, this

3. RockMagnetism
Hysteresisparameters,theacquisitionofisothermalremanentmagnetization(IRM),andback‐fielddemag-
netizationofsaturationIRMweremeasured.Thesestrong‐fieldmeasurementswerecompletedusingavari-
able field translation balance at the Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences,
China(IGGCAS)oraPrincetonMeasurementsCorporationModel3900‐4vibratingsamplemagnetometer
attheUtahPaleomagneticCenter,UniversityofUtah,USA(UPC).Magneticsusceptibility(MS)versustem-
peraturecurveswereacquiredwithaKappabridgeKLY‐4Sinstrument(IGGCAS)oranAGICOMFK1‐FA
(UPC).ThemagneticpropertiesofallthesamplesfromsectionAweremeasuredattheIGGCAS,whereas
samplesfromsectionBweremeasuredattheUPC.
3.1. RoomTemperatureRemanenceExperiments
Room temperature hysteresis loops and backfield curves were measured for 48 representative specimens.
Hysteresisloopsfor40samplesare“wasp‐waisted”(Figures3a–3f),suggestingthedistributionofasinglemag-
neticcomponentwithdifferentmagneticdomainsizes(Dunlop,2002)ormultiplemagneticcomponentseach
withcontrastingcoercivities(Robertsetal.,1995;Tauxeetal.,1996).TheB andB valuesaremainly100–500 c cr
mT,indicatingthedominantmagneticcarrierhasahighcoercivity(Figures3a–3eand4a‐4e).IRMacquisition
curvesforthesesamplesdonotreachfullsaturationevenat1.5Tor2.0T(Figures4a–4f).Afewsamplesshow
gradualincreasesinacquiredremanenceandjustreach<20%saturationbelow200mT(Figures4aand4b).
Thisobservationsuggestslimitedcontributionsoflow‐coercivitymagneticcarriersinthesespecimens.The
acquisitioncurvesofsomesamplestypicallyexhibitarapidincreaseandreachmorethan50%saturationbelow
200mT(Figures4c–4f),implyingahigherconcentrationoflow‐coercivitymagneticcarriersinthesespecimens.

3.2. ThermomagneticExperiments
Wemeasuredthelow‐fieldsusceptibility(κ)asafunctionofhigh‐temperature(T)for17representativespeci-
mens.Resultsfromtheseκ‐Texperimentstypicallyshowtwophasesofdistinctdecreasesinκwithincreasing
temperatureatapproximatelyboth680°Cand580°C(Figures5a–5e).Thismagneticbehaviorisconsistent
withthepresenceofhematiteandmagnetiteinthesespecimens.Coolingcurvesforsomespecimensshow
large increases in susceptibility (Figures 5d and 5e); this might be the result of thermal alteration of
Fe‐bearingmineralsduringheating,forexampledehydrationofclaysorexsolutionofFe‐richandTi‐rich
end‐membermineralogiesfromtheoriginalironoxidesintheselavas.Somespecimensalsoexhibitasingle
distinct change in magnetic susceptibility at approximately 580 °C, indicating a major presence of
magnetite(Figure5f).
4. Magnetic Petrography andGeochemistry
Photomicrographs of some representative samples in transmitted polarizing light reveal that most rocks
havepilotaxitictextureswithplagioclasemicrocrystalsrandomlydistributedthroughtherocks(Figure6).
Microcrystallinepyroxene,volcanicglasses,andopaqueminerals(magnetiteandhematite)areinterstitial
betweenplagioclases.Mostofthethinsectionsshowlittlesignofstrongalteration.

We made thorough microscopic observations on representative samples fromsites Qyc01, Qyc02,Qyc06,
andQyc07withanelectronmicroprobeanalyzer(EMPA)(JXA‐8230,JEOL,Japan)setinback‐scattering
electron imaging mode. These measurements were completed at the Key Laboratory of Continental
CollisionandPlateauUplift,InstituteofTibetanPlateauResearch,ChineseAcademyofSciences,Beijing,
China.Wealsoanalyzedelementalcompositionofsomegrainsinthinsectionsusingenergydispersivespec-
trometryintheEMPA.
SamplesfromSitesQyc01,Qyc02,Qyc06,andQyc07containmicrocrystallinelathesofplagioclasewithfine‐
grainedinterstitialFe‐bearingminerals(Figure7).MostoftheseFe‐bearingmineralsareirregularinshape,
rangeinsizefrom~5to50μm,andlackobviouslyoxidizedrimsandshrinkagecracks(Figures7a–7h).In
sampleQyc06‐4,somemicrocrystallineneedle‐shapedgrainsweidentifyashematiteareeuhedralwithcrys-
talsizesbetween2–5μm(Figure7e).InsampleQyc07‐7,thehematitelamellaecrystals,whicharelessthan
1μmwide,appeartobeexsolvedfromsphene(Figure7i);thistextureisconsistentwithhigh‐temperature
oxidation.TheFe‐bearingmineralsobservedinthinsectionhavemorphologiesconsistentwithmagmatic
origins,incontrasttoformationfromweathering.EnergydispersivespectrometryandEMPAanalysesalso
showthattheseFe‐bearingmineralshaveTicontentslessthan4%(Figures7j–7l).ThelowTiconcentrations
suggest that the Fe‐oxides in these lavas did not form from primary Ti‐rich titanomagnetite by low‐
temperatureoxidationprocesseslongaftercooling.Instead,thesepetrographicobservationsandgeochem-
icaldata,whencombinedwiththerockmagneticdata,suggestthathematiteandmagnetiteformedfrom
high‐temperatureexsolutionduringorshortlyafterinitialcooling(Geissman&VanderVoo,1980).Ifthis
interpretationiscorrect,thenweshouldexpecthematiteandmagnetitetocarrythesamehigh‐temperature
remanencedirection.

Weplottedourdemagnetizationresultsonorthogonalvectordiagramsandcalculateddirectionsusingprin-

values of ChRM directions are <15°; (2) site‐mean directions are calculated from five or more samples;

WefollowtheinterpretationsfromtheTimeAveragedGeomagneticFieldInitiativethatvirtualgeomag-
neticpoles(VGPs)morelikelyfitaFisheriandistributionthansitemeandirections(e.g.,Cromwelletal.,

andthencalculatedthelocalitymeanVGP.Thelocalitymeandirectionsandtheiruncertaintiesarecalcu-

groupmeanmethodtoreduceredundantsampling(i.e.,oversampling)ofsecularvariation(Lippertetal.,

andaFishergroupmeandirectioniscalculatedfromallsamplesinthegroupedsite(Chenetetal.,2008;
Lippertetal.,2011).

Wealsonotethattheserocksdonotshowevidenceoflow‐temperatureoxidationoftheFe‐oxidesinthin
section. If the magnetite and hematite did indeed acquire their remanence during high‐temperature
oxidation during initial cooling of the lavas, then the directions should be similar. That they are slightly
different could be the result of differences in the duration of remanence acquisition during cooling. The
residual remanence intensity above 580 °C versus NRM intensity (Int /Int ) of the 182 samples
580 NRM
containinghematiterevealstwomajorpopulationsofsamples:oneintherangeof0.2–0.4andtheother
0.8–1.0,withanaveragevalueof0.65(FigureS1).Consideringthesaturationmagnetizationofhematiteis
~200 times weaker than that of magnetite, the abundance of hematite in our samples should be much
higher than that of magnetite. If the hematite was transformed from primary Ti‐rich titanomagnetite by
low‐temperatureoxidationprocesses,thenwewouldexpecttoseewildlydistributedoxidationstructures,
yet we do not (Figures 6 and 7). These observations provide evidence that both magnetite and hematite
wereproducedbyhigh‐temperatureexsolutionduringinitialcoolingofthelava,aninterpretationthatis
alsosupportedbyourmagneticpetrographyandgeochemistryresults(Figures6and7).

Therefore,weconcludethatthemagnetizationpreservedintheMiddleTriassiclavaswasacquiredprior
tofolding.
ThemeasuredbeddingattitudesforlocalitiesAandBsuggestthatthesamplingareacontainsaplunging
fold.Wecannotruleoutthisinterpretationwithourcurrentfieldobservations.Wenotethatdifferencein
bedding attitudes alternatively might be caused by local rotations, because some strike‐like faults and
normalorthrustfaultsareobservedinthesamplingarea(Figure1b).Ifweassumethereisaplungingfold
axis,thentheFisherprecisionparameter(k)ofthemeanofsitemeandirectionsimprovesfrom36.0°to43.9°
afteraplungingfoldcorrectionisapplied.Thelocality‐meandeclinationsbetweensectionsAandBare36.0°
and14.0°,respectively,buttheinclinationsare40.0°and39.6°.Whentheplungingfoldcorrectionisapplied,
thegroupmeandeclinationforbothsectionsvariesfrom29.2°to31.2°.However,theinclinationstillvaries
from39.9°to40.1°.Thus,thedifferenceindeclinationscanbeattributedtoeitheraplungingfoldaxisorto
small local rotations; both interpretations are consistent and permissible with our field observations and
satelliteobservations.Theapparentrotationsareminorandwedonothaveenoughsitemeandirections
from each locality to sample secular variation and calculate robust section poles to quantify the rotation
between localities. Regardless of the source of dispersion in the sampling location declinations, both the
plungingfoldcorrectionandtherotationcorrectionshavenoappreciableeffectontheresultingstudymean
inclinationfromwhichwewilldirectlycalculatethepaleolatitude.Thatis,thechoiceofstructuralinterpre-
tationandcorrectionofthestudiedsectionshasnoappreciableeffectononeoftheprincipalgoalsofour
study:thepaleolatitudeofthenorthernQiangtangblock.
The 20 group mean directions from the two sections yield a VGP dispersion of 13.9° (95% uncertainty
interval is between 13.2° and 14.6°) at ~ 23°N, consistent with the Sλ = 14.5° (limits between 13.8° and
15.2°)dispersionobservedintheVGPdatabaseof0–5Malavasatasimilarlatitude(Johnsonetal.,2008).
TheA valueofourdatasetis5.6°,whichisintherangeofvaluesthatareestimatedtoaveragepaleosecular
95
variation (5.1–12.4°, Deenen et al., 2011). Field observations show that the lavas are interbedded with
sedimentarylayers(Figure2).Inconclusion,theMean‐IIprimaryremanencedirectionsappeartoaverage
secularvariationandthereforearesuitableforpaleogeographicreconstructions.
6. Discussion
6.1. MiddleTriassicLatitudeoftheNorthernQiangtangBlock
WeconcludethatourChRMdirectionsfromthe20groupmeandirectionsfromtheMiddleTriassiclavas
describedaboverecordaprimarythermoremanentmagnetization.Thisinterpretationisbasedonthefol-
lowingobservations:(1)apositivefoldtestathighconfidence,consistentwithaprefoldingmagnetization;
(2)ChRMscarriedbybothmagnetiteandhematite;(3)high‐temperatureChRMdirectionscarriedbyhema-
titeandmagnetitearesimilar;and(4)anabsenceofrockmagnetic,petrographic,orpaleomagneticevidence
thatsuggeststhatunremovedorsecondarymagnetizationsbiastheChRMdirections.Thedistributionof
VGPsisconsistentwiththeinterpretationthatourdatasetsamplespaleosecularvariationandcanprovide
astatisticallyrigorousestimateofthetime‐averagedfieldduringtheeruptionofthelavas.Insummary,our
data yield a Fisher mean paleopole located at 62.2°N, 196.4°E (A = 5.6°, K = 34.3, S = 13.9°), which 95
corresponds to a latitude of 23.0 ± 5.6 °N for our sampling locality (33.5°N, 92.0°E) of the northern
Qiangtangblock.
6.2. PaleomagneticConstraintsontheClosureofthePaleo‐TethysOcean
In the following discussion, the expected dipole paleolatitudes at a reference site in northern Qiangtang
(33.5°N,92.0°E)werecalculatedfromeachpaleomagneticpolethatsatisfiesourdataqualitycriteria.Wefol-
lowed the data selection criteria described in Song et al. (2017) to classify the published pre‐Cretaceous
paleomagneticdatafromthenorthernQiangtangblockintodataqualitybins.ClassAdataaredistinguished
by(1)evidenceforaprimaryremanence(positivefoldtestorreversalstest);(2)ameanVGPthatiscalcu-
lated from more than 10 or 100 sample/site/group mean directions for lavas or sediments, respectively;

fromMiddleTriassicrocksshowthatnorthernQiangtangwaslocatedat~23.0±5.6°Nat~240Maforthe
reference point (33.5°N, 92.0°E). Ma et al. (1993), Tan et al. (1991), and Yang et al. (1991) measured
threepaleopolesfromMiddleTriassicrocksfromtheShanxiareaoftheNCBthatareconsistentwitheach
other. We calculated a mean paleopole of 1.6°N, 61.6°E, with A = 4.2° by averaging these three poles;
95
thispoleprovidesapaleolatitudeof28.9±4.2°NfortheNCBduringtheMiddleTriassicforthereference
point(33.5°N,92.0°E).TherearenopublishedpaleopolesfortheMiddleTriassicofTarim,soweusedthe
spline apparent polar wander paths of Wu et al. (2017) to estimate the paleolatitude of the southern
margin of Tarim: ~29.9 ± 3.1°N at ~240 Ma. Thus, we estimate that the remnant Paleo‐Tethys Ocean
realm or Songpan‐Ganzi back‐arc ocean basin was ~5.9 ± 7.0 to 6.9 ± 6.4° of latitude, or ~650 ± 770 to
760 ± 700 km wide at ~240 Ma (Figures 10 and 11). Although the uncertainty in these calculations
permit that the Paleo‐Tethys Ocean was closed by Middle Triassic time, the abundance of Late‐
Triassic deep‐marine sediments that outcrop in the Hoh Xil‐Songpan‐Gangzi basin (Ding et al., 2013;
Yin & Nie, 1993) require that an ocean existed between the northern Qiangtang block and the
Tarim‐NCB collage in Middle Triassic.

### page_16
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2019JB017804
paleomagnetic data from NCB and Tarim (Fang et al., 1990; Ma et al.,
1993; McFadden et al., 1988; Yang et al., 1991; Tan et al., 1991; Wu
et al., 1990; Zhao et al., 1996) or with the apparent polar wander paths
for NCB‐Tarim (Wu et al., 2017), show that latitudes of northern
Qiangtang overlap with these of NCB‐Tarim by the latest Triassic
(~215Ma)andatthelatitudeof~31.0°N(Figures10and11).Thisimplies
that the northern Qiangtang block collided with Eurasia during
thelatestTriassic.
A latest Triassic collision as estimated from paleomagnetic data is
consistent with several geological observations which suggest final
collision and suturing of the northern Qiangtang block to southern
Eurasia between 220 and 200 Ma. The deformation of the Hoh Xil‐
Songpan‐Ganzi turbidites is associated with ~230–200 Ma granites with
postorogenic chemistries (Burchfiel et al., 1995; Harrowfield & Wilson,
2005;Reid,Fowler,etal.,2005,Reid,Wilson,etal.,2005).Intheinternal
domain of the Hoh Xil – Songpan‐Ganzi orogenic wedge, the deforma-
tion associated with Barrovian‐type metamorphism (5–7 kbar and
400–600 °C) is dated to 220–190 Ma (Huang et al., 2003). Nonmarine
deposition in and around the Hoh Xil‐Songpan‐Ganzi basin began in
the Late Triassic‐Early Jurassic (Ding et al., 2013; Yin & Nie, 1993).
The drastic change in detrital zircon provenance in the Hoh
Xil‐Songpan‐Ganzi basin from a Middle Triassic source area in North
China to a Late Triassic source on the Yangtze craton, the rotation of
theSouthChinablock,andthethickeningoftheaccretionaryprismsug-
gest a Late‐Triassic closure of the Hoh Xil ‐ Songpan‐Ganzi basin
(Bruguieretal.,1997; Rogeretal.,2008).
Three other Permian‐Triassic paleopoles from the northern Qiangtang
block also meet the requirements for Class A data: the ~297 Ma pole
from Song et al. (2017), the ~259 Ma pole from Ma et al. (2019), and
the~210MapolefromSongetal.(2015)(Table2).Thelatitudinaltrend
of all four Permian‐Triassic Class A data suggest that the northern
Qiangtang block drifted to Northern Hemisphere subtropical paleolati-
tudes between ~300 and 240 Ma and transited approximately 46° of
latitudeinthattime(Figures10).Thistrend,whichissupportedbymore
than half of the Class B data, suggests an average northward conver-

7. Conclusions
Newpaleomagneticdirectionsweremeasuredfrom28MiddleTriassicvolcanicsitesaroundtheYanshiping
townonthenorthernQiangtangblock.Noobviousrockmagnetic,petrographic,orpaleomagneticobserva-
tionsindicatethatthe28sitemeanChRMsdirectionsareinfluencedbyunremovedorsecondarymagneti-
zations.Furthermore,ourdatapassfoldtestsandappeartoaveragesecularvariation.Ourpaleomagnetic
datafromMiddleTriassiclavaslocatethenorthernQiangtangblockat23.0±5.6°Nat~240Maatourrefer-
encelocation(33.5°N,92.0°E).AcomparisonofthepaleomagneticdatafromtheMiddleTriassicrockson
the NCB to our results from northern Qiangtang indicates that the remnant Paleo‐Tethys Ocean or
Songpan‐Ganziback‐arcoceanbasincouldhavebeenupto∼700kmwideduringtheMiddleTriassic.A
comparisonoftheTriassiclatitudinalhistoryofthenorthernQiangtangblocktotheNCB‐Tarimcollagesug-
geststhatthenorthernQiangtangblocksuturedtoEurasiaduringthelatestTriassic.Ourcompilationof
publishedpaleomagneticdatafromthenorthernQiangtangblockshowsthatitsnorth‐southconvergence
ratetowardEurasiadecreasedfrom~8.5cm/yrto~3.6cm/yraroundorbefore240Ma.Wehypothesizethat
thisdecelerationwascausedbyanarc‐continentcollisionbetweenthePaleo‐TethysorYidunarcandnorth-
ernQiangtangblockpriortothefinalclosureofthePaleo‐TethysOcean.
